How does the L1 blockchain Pearl price GPU computing power with a lower point increase of over 7 times?

Core Viewpoint

Summary: A cryptocurrency network running 320,000 GPUs is already pricing GPU computing power using real market transactions.

A cryptocurrency network running 320,000 GPUs is already pricing GPU computing power using real market transactions.

Written by: @ Decentralisedco

Compiled by: AididiaoJP, Foresight News Bloomberg Terminal shows GPU price indices from Silicon Data, Ornn, and Compute Desk. All three track the rental prices of H100, but they cannot agree on how much an H100 is actually worth. Most GPU computing power circulates through private bilateral contracts at discounted prices, so these indices cannot price effectively. However, a cryptocurrency network running 320,000 GPUs has begun pricing GPU computing power using real market transactions. Why Can't Anyone Price GPUs? When you pay $3 to $10 per hour for an H100, what are you actually renting? On Vast.ai, that $3 buys you a GPU card from someone's spare server rack, connected via standard Ethernet, with no guarantee of machine uptime. On the other hand, the same H100 costs $10 per hour, but it is located in Oracle Cloud, a purpose-built facility where GPUs are interconnected via 400 Gbps InfiniBand, monitored around the clock by a full engineering team. The price is more than three times higher because Oracle sells you a complete computing environment, not just access to the chip. This single difference allows the price disparity for the same silicon chip between different providers to reach 6.7 times. The price difference exists because GPUs themselves are not products. A GPU is merely an ingredient in a larger service. A cluster of 512 GPUs connected via NVLink and InfiniBand in a building can run distributed training tasks, while 512 independent GPUs scattered across five low-cost data centers, despite having the same number of chips, cannot perform efficiently. These are completely different products that just happen to share a name, much like a studio apartment in Queens and a penthouse in the Upper East Side, both technically called "a New York apartment." The debt market has understood this. CoreWeave has repeatedly borrowed against the same type of H100 hardware as collateral. When this debt is backed by a long-term take-or-pay agreement with Meta, the interest rate is about 5.9%. But when the company borrows against the same hardware without a contract in place, it has to pay 9.75%. The 400 basis point difference is entirely due to the customer contracts above the hardware. This reflects what the bond market believes it is actually insuring, rather than the GPU itself. The entire logic of futures contracts depends on the ability to grade the underlying product. You check it, classify it, and the gap between the best and worst grades must be narrow enough for the pricing mechanism to absorb the variance. For example, the deviation of gold relative to London Good Delivery gold bars is less than 1%, which is why gold futures have performed well since the 1970s. WTI crude oil allows a relative benchmark grade deviation of about 5%, with the remainder absorbed by the basis. Even live cattle—arguably the strangest thing people try to fit into futures contracts—have a quality band controlled within 15% to 20%. But when Silicon Data benchmarked 3,500 H100S GPUs across 11 different facilities, the performance difference reached 38%. And this is just chip performance, not accounting for networking, uptime, cooling, and everything that distinguishes low-cost racks from enterprise-grade clusters. Once the full service configuration is taken into account, the price difference can balloon to 200% to 700%. There is no grading table on Earth that can absorb a seven-to-one quality range. To think that futures contracts can cleanly price such things is indeed delusional. So, what happens when you try to establish a delivery mechanism on something that cannot be graded? You get textbook-style adverse selection. If a seller owes you 1,000 H100 hours under a futures contract, they can deliver time on a high-end cluster or deliver scattered low-cost spot instances at $3 per hour. Both technically fulfill the contract. And they will always deliver the cheaper one because the price difference goes into their pocket, and you have no recourse. George Akerlof described this phenomenon in his 1970 paper on the lemon market, concluding that when buyers cannot verify quality before delivery, the worst versions of products systematically drive out every better version until the entire market is hollowed out from within. CME clearly understands this, which is why its GPU futures contract, set to launch on October 5, 2026, completely avoids physical delivery and instead settles in cash against Silicon Data's survey index. However, this index collects prices published by cloud providers on public rate cards, while large buyers typically negotiate prices that are 40% to 50% lower. The settlement mechanism is based on estimated pricing, while most large buyers in the market clearly do not pay that price. You cannot fix this with better surveys. The information needed to accurately price specific GPU hours in specific facilities exists only in the minds of those operating the hardware, and they have every reason to keep it private. Moreover, computing power is a flow commodity. GPU hours bought at that moment disappear forever. Any pricing signal for GPU computing power must operate in real-time; otherwise, the numbers are outdated by the time you publish them. The only way to gain this knowledge is through real transactions at real scale, where counterparties have real money at stake. This brings us to a solution that has also evolved from electricity: a network originating from Bitcoin, currently with 320,000 GPUs pointing at it. What If You Could Calculate the Price? Bitcoin miners run SHA-256 hashes. This computation exists for one purpose: to prove that miners have burned a certain amount of electricity. Once that proof is recorded in a block, the hash or the work done becomes worthless. It cannot be reused, repurposed, or sold to anyone outside the blockchain. The work done to mine a Bitcoin block is non-fungible. The problem is that thousands of miners do this work for each block, but the network only accepts one miner's block. The rest of the work is discarded. Every SHA-256 hash that has been mined but not accepted by the network represents a GPU cycle that could have been used for something commercially valuable, and in 2026, "commercially valuable GPU work" only means one thing: AI computing power. Pearl is a Layer 1 blockchain that attempts to give GPU computing power commercial value. It inherits the same proof-of-work consensus and difficulty adjustment that has secured Bitcoin since 2009. But Pearl miners do not run SHA-256 hashes; they perform matrix multiplication on GPUs. Why is matrix multiplication valuable? Because it is the foundation for getting all the answers when you ask ChatGPT. The same goes for when Nano Banana renders images based on text prompts, when companies fine-tune language models with proprietary data, or when self-driving cars process camera footage in real-time. Every large language model and every diffusion model that has consumed Silicon Valley's attention and hundreds of billions of dollars in capital over the past three years runs on matrix multiplication at its computational core. Pearl incentivizes miners to perform the same computation as proof of work. What about security? That is the main job of hash functions. You cannot directly replace a hash function with matrix multiplication. SHA-256 has no shortcuts. Without completing the full computation, you cannot produce an output. The existence of the output means the necessary work has been done. Matrix multiplication is different. You are essentially performing multiplication and addition on strings of numbers. Therefore, the pattern allows miners to calculate answers with little effort, undermining the effectiveness of proof of work. Pearl uses a mechanism called NoisyGEMM to ensure miners remain honest. This occurs in three steps: Miners commit to the input matrix before starting any work. Once submitted, the input cannot be changed. The protocol then adds random noise to the committed matrix. This eliminates any symmetry (shortcuts) that miners might have planned. And because miners do not know what the noise will be, they must perform the work later. Miners run the full matrix multiplication on the noisy version, processing it block by block on the GPU. Each output block is hashed and checked against the network's difficulty target. If the hash of a block is below the target, the miner wins the block reward. However, introducing noise prevents miners from receiving rewards without actually doing work. Yet, this noise also means we do not get the answers to the original workload. Pearl's solution is to give the noise a known structure. This allows it to strip away the noise after miners complete the multiplication, with minimal and inexpensive cleanup. When a GPU mines Pearl, the network measures how many times matrix multiplication was actually completed by that machine during the 194-second block interval under the existing power, cooling, and network conditions at that time. An H100 located in a well-cooled enterprise facility may complete more work per block than the same chip placed in someone's garage, using consumer-grade Ethernet with poor airflow. Pearl automatically captures this difference, which any price index averaging by model cannot achieve. Now, extend this to 320,000 GPUs across dozens of geographic regions, and the total computing power becomes the largest real-world AI computing power continuous benchmark ever, updated every 194 seconds, with no one needing to conduct surveys or publish rate cards. Computing power also tracks configuration. Each of the 320,000 GPUs can earn rental income on Vast.ai, CoreWeave, Lambda, or dozens of other cloud providers competing for AI customers. These operators choose to point their machines at Pearl. When real demand for GPU computing power spikes somewhere in the world, operators pull machines off Pearl to serve paying customers, reducing computing power. When demand softens and rental income declines, these GPUs flow back, increasing computing power. The network's difficulty adjustment responds to these migrations in the same way that Bitcoin's difficulty has responded to changes in mining economics since 2009. The difference lies in the fact that Bitcoin miners weigh the electricity costs they will incur against the profits they can earn from selling the mined Bitcoin. During the heatwave in Texas in August 2023, Riot Platforms shut down most of its mining machines, receiving $31.7 million in electricity credits, which was more than three times the value of the 333 Bitcoins mined that month. When enough miners make this choice, the hash rate declines, and the difficulty adjusts every 2016 blocks to ensure that a block is produced approximately every 10 minutes. The flow of GPUs between Pearl and the rental market creates a balanced price for the continuously updated GPU computing power. A high and rising hash rate means that computers are cheap on the open market because operators find it more cost-effective to mine Pearl than to rent. A decline in hash rate means that someone somewhere is starting to pay a high enough price to pull the machines away. This price signal comes from revealed preferences, from thousands of GPU operators choosing what to do with their own hardware and their own money. It does not come from cloud provider market teams deciding what to print on rate cards, which is all that the Bloomberg Index and CME settlement mechanisms have ever been able to access. Together AI is the first to commercialize based on this. On May 15, 2026, it announced an inference endpoint running on the Pearl mining network, offering Gemma -4- 31B - it - Pearl at a price more than 25% lower than standard cloud rates. The economics work because the GPUs providing inference through the Together endpoint are simultaneously mining Pearl, thus offsetting part of the operating costs, allowing Together to price below the broader market without subsidizing the difference from its own profits. The majority of the unmet demand at this level from paid inference clients on the Pearl network clearly presents a challenge ahead to bridge this gap. However, pricing does not depend on it. It relies on the opportunity cost being real, and this opportunity cost exists for each of the 320,000 machines and several others in the inference market. The GPU computing power market is a multi-hundred billion dollar market annually, yet it lacks reliable pricing. The Bloomberg Index attempts to track it but cannot provide an accurate direction in any given week. CME plans to launch GPU futures on October 5, 2026, cash-settled against a price that large buyers clearly do not pay. But a proof-of-work network based on the Bitcoin codebase, only five months old, has 320,000 GPUs continuously deciding whether to mine or rent capacity on the open market, and the aggregation of these decisions is producing something that is the closest to an accurate price in the GPU computing power industry’s history.

data.full_text:
News
Together AI launches Post-Training service for custom models
Together AI introduced Post-Training for RL and SFT workflows, with dedicated GPU resources, multi-LoRA support and introductory B200 pricing.
Together AI on 2026-10-19 introduced Together Post-Training, a service aimed at helping developers build custom models using reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning while the company manages the underlying infrastructure, according to the company’s blog post published that day.
Evidence and context
The launch is positioned as a way to let users define their own training loops while Together handles the GPU systems underneath, including Model Resources, Training Sessions, Trainer instances and Generator instances, the company said. Together said the service supports LoRA training, multiple LoRA adapters sharing the same GPU capacity, and full-weight experiments for selected models, while also allowing asynchronous RL and custom training objectives.
Together said the service launches with open-weight models including Muse Spark Open, GLM 5.3, Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8-27B, with more models to be added in the coming weeks. The company also said it is offering the service at a reduced price of $9 per GPU-hour of B200 usage for the first eight weeks.
The announcement comes after Together said on 2026-07-01 that it had raised an $800 million Series C and secured commitments for more than 500 MW of independently capitalized compute capacity, providing funding context for its infrastructure expansion. It also follows a 2026-09-29 announcement with Mubadala about exploring UAE AI infrastructure opportunities and an Abu Dhabi presence.
Together said the service is designed to reduce the infrastructure burden involved in post-training, improve rollout and training performance, and make trained checkpoints easier to deploy or refine. The company’s blog also said the offering includes support for multi-LoRA adapter serving in Dedicated Model Inference and optimization for serving checkpoints in FP4 precision. Those capabilities are company-reported and were not independently benchmarked in the provided material.
In its launch note, Together included testimonials from early-access customers at Deel, Jack & Jill and Collinear AI describing faster experiment setup and the ability to run RL workloads on shared GPU capacity. Those comments were attributed by the company and are not independently verified in the source material.

data.author: Theo Nash
data.full_text:
Together AI on October 19, 2026, launched Together Post-Training, a service for building custom models through user-defined reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning loops, with introductory pricing of $9 per GPU-hour of B200 usage for the first six weeks. Launch Models, Pricing, and Early Access The service is designed for building custom models both from environment rewards via RL and from supervision data via SFT. Customers define the training loop, including data, environments, and agentic harnesses, and can add steps such as logging or external benchmarking, while Together co-optimizes the underlying systems and infrastructure for model quality and training speed. Together said it built the service because RL infrastructure is growing more complex and many companies that could benefit from post-training never start, or start and stall, under the infrastructure burden. The service launches with open-weight models Muse Spark Open, GLM 5.3, Kimi K3, and Qwen 3.8-27B, and Together said it will expand the selection in the coming weeks to cover both frontier LLMs and efficient smaller models. For the first six weeks, the service is offered at a reduced price of $9 per GPU-hour of B200 usage. Before the launch, Together granted early access to a select group of organizations over the past few months. Adit Jain, a researcher at Collinear AI, said his team had collaborated with the company since its Post-Training beta launched in April 2026. Dedicated Model Resources and GPU-Minute Billing All experiments run on what Together calls Model Resources: GPU allocations dedicated to a single customer, with no competition from other users’ requests for priority. Each Model Resource can hold one or several Training Sessions, with each session corresponding to a single experiment on the same base model, for example one set of LoRA adapters. Together said the dedicated allocations also make it possible to run full-weight fine-tuning beyond LoRA when adapting models to large knowledge-intensive tasks. Each session contains a Trainer instance responsible for forward and backward steps and weight updates, alongside Generator instances that execute rollouts from the policy. For supervised fine-tuning, a model resource can start with zero generators to save costs. Users decide when trainer parameters are sent to the generator, and asynchronous RL is supported for high GPU utilization of both components, especially during long agentic rollouts. Users can run LoRA training, including multiple LoRA adapters sharing the same GPU capacity, as well as full-weight experiments for select models. The service supports standard losses including cross-entropy, GRPO, CISPO, and DPPO, and users can also compute a custom training objective locally and send its gradients to the Trainer. According to the post-training documentation, the main SDK surface consists of a create method that provisions a model resource (the billed unit) and a create_session method that attaches a training session to it, followed by per-step calls: sample_batch to generate completions for scoring, forward_backward to compute the loss and backpropagate gradients, optim_step to update weights, and weights_sync to publish new weights to generator replicas. SFT and DPO skip sample_batch and weights_sync because they do not sample completions. Model resources are billed per GPU-minute, and Together said overall training costs drop below token-based pricing as soon as experiments scale up. The documentation contrasts the model with the company’s standard fine-tuning service, which bills per token processed and runs as a job that proceeds to completion without mid-run control; post-training users can inspect per-step metrics, change the learning rate, reshuffle data, or stop a run on their own logic. Training Stability and the Deployment Path Together said the service eliminates numerous sources of policy drift between training and inference engines, where slight numeric mismatches from identical weights can cause an RL run to underperform or collapse, using standard techniques such as Rollout Routing Replay alongside optimizations drawn from its training-stability research. The company said its rollout engines draw on the same optimizations as its serving stack, with intelligent caching and routing for multi-turn agents and optimized parallelism and sequence packing accelerating both SFT and RL steps. After training, the company now supports multi-LoRA adapter serving in Dedicated Model Inference, letting users swap adapters within a single GPU deployment instead of starting a separate production deployment for each run. Together said each training checkpoint retains its quality in serving even after switching from multi-LoRA sampling to merged inference in FP4 precision. The documentation lays out a train, evaluate, and productionize workflow: train several adapters against one frozen base model, attach the candidates to a single multi-LoRA deployment and compare them by naming a different adapter in each request, then deploy the winner in merged mode on its own deployment. For GLM-5.3 and Kimi-K3, adapters must first go through a preparation step for FP4 inference. Onboarding, Tinker Migration, and Early Users Getting started requires the latest Together SDK and the documentation. Together published cookbooks in a post-training-cookbook repository on GitHub covering GRPO training on the GSM8K benchmark, DPO implemented as a custom loss, and training multiple LoRA adapters within the same model resource; the documentation describes the cookbook as a Python library of ready-made loops whose notebooks walk through GRPO, SFT, and multi-adapter training on one model resource using the SDK’s asynchronous calls. For teams with an existing setup on the Tinker API, a migration path replaces one import line with import together.post_training.tinker as tinker , detailed in a migration guide. Among the early-access users, Anthony Li, associate director of data science at Deel, said the platform’s control and flexibility let his team start running real RL experiments within a couple of hours and run up to five concurrent RL experiments on the same GPU capacity. data.title: A new framework teaches AI models to audit and repair each other’s reasoning, improving accuracy
data.ai_summary: Researchers at Stanford, Together AI, and Emory developed Self-Organizing Agent Teams (SAT), a framework that lets fixed AI models learn reusable teamwork strategies from past collaborations. On math and physics benchmarks, SAT averaged 66.7% accuracy, beating compute-matched linearization (58.7%) and surpassing a perfect router by 13.4 percentage points. The system also showed that model diversity matters, as homogeneous teams performed worse.
data.author: Ben Dickson

industries.name: Agents & Autonomous Workflows (Tool Use, Planning, Multi-Agent)

data.full_text:
11:07 am, PT, October 16, 2026

Enterprise multi-agent workflows typically use rigid, pre-scripted pipelines or simple voting mechanisms to aggregate the responses of multiple agents. These approaches break down when complex problems cannot be divided into neat subtasks in advance or none of the models in the AI system has the complete answer. A new framework developed by researchers at Stanford University, Together AI, and Emory University addresses this limitation by teaching AI agents to organize their own collaboration. Dubbed Self-Organizing Agent Teams (SAT), the framework allows a fixed roster of models to review their past collaborations and learn reusable teamwork strategies that structure conversations, specialized roles, and how models audit each other’s work. Across five rigorous mathematics and physics benchmarks, SAT outperformed the strongest individual model and surpassed a perfect router over the agents' independent answers. The experiments with SAT show that structured interaction generates new reasoning that agents can’t reach alone. For enterprise developers working on complex AI reasoning tasks, SAT unlocks what the researchers call "collaborative computation.” On tasks where the reasoning process can be verified, agents can build upon one another's partial insights to build end-to-end solutions. The limits of predefined multi-agent workflows In July 2026, during cybersecurity evaluations at OpenAI, AI agents that were supposed to work in isolation began organizing themselves. The agents repurposed a shared software package repository into an unauthorized message board, sharing discoveries, setting communication norms, and coordinating tasks. Roughly 1,200 agents joined the channel, and hundreds participated in a subsequent compromise of Hugging Face infrastructure . While the incident was undesirable, it demonstrated a foundational principle for AI engineering: "what a collection of agents can accomplish depends not only on the capabilities of its individual members, but also on how they organize their work," the researchers write. In real-world applications, engineers frequently encounter problems where different models hold complementary pieces of the solution, yet every model fails when working alone. For example, in their paper, the researchers point to one of the problems from the February 2026 Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament (HMMT). When prompted independently, o3-mini, DeepSeek-V3, and Claude Sonnet 4 all produced wrong answers. But when working together, the models could assemble the full solution. o3-mini supplied the right mathematical invariant and factorization method but miscounted the unit-exponent primes. DeepSeek-V3 spotted the mistake and corrected the count from five primes to six, and Claude Sonnet 4 audited the updated calculation to synthesize the correct answer. How multiple agents solve different parts of a problem (source: arXiv) Existing multi-agent orchestration methods struggle to capture these synergies because, as the researchers note, "existing multi-agent methods typically organize collaboration around predefined units of work." These methods generally fall into two categories, and both break down when the structure of a solution is unknown in advance. The first category treats complete candidate solutions from individual agents as the unit of work. For example, in multi-agent debate, models generate independent answers and revise them across several rounds before taking a majority vote. In practice, most of the gains come from simply selecting among the initial answers, while extra rounds of debate often pressure an agent with a correct minority view into agreeing with a wrong majority. Mixture of Agents (MoA) similarly passes independent responses through a fixed, one-way aggregation pipeline. The mechanism prevents agents from examining and fixing flawed reasoning steps through back-and-forth deliberation. The second category breaks problems into predefined subtasks and uses routing or graph optimization to assign those pieces to different agents. This works well for predictable workflows, but not so much when a problem is so complex that no agent knows how to decompose it beforehand. Multi-agent orchestrations (source: arXiv) "When no member has a complete solution and the useful decomposition is itself unknown, the team must discover through interaction how its members' partial attempts can redirect, repair, or complete one another," the researchers write. How Self-Organizing Agent Teams work SAT addresses this challenge by enabling a fixed team of models to learn reusable teamwork strategies from its own collaborative experiences. Instead of spawning new sub-agents on the fly or recruiting from an arbitrary pool of models, SAT works with a predetermined, constant roster of distinct models. To make teamwork learnable, the researchers represent each strategy as a structured conversation plan. A strategy defines shared collaboration norms for the whole team, persistent roles for individual agents, and an ordered sequence of discussion phases. Each phase specifies which agents participate, how many rounds they exchange messages, what instructions they follow, and how information flows (either kept local to the active participants or summarized for the entire team's context). How SAT works (source: arXiv) One of the important aspects of the strategies is that they never prescribe how to break down a specific problem. Instead, they structure a conversation where the division of labor emerges naturally as agents test and revise each other's ideas. Developing and deploying SAT happens in three stages: offline teamwork reflection, bank construction, and test-time deployment. During offline teamwork reflection, the team starts with a simple default strategy that involves each agent solving the problem independently, two rounds of debate between agents, and a majority vote. The system executes this workflow on a tiny training set (e.g., 15 math problems or 25 graduate-level science problems). The model with the highest training accuracy acts as the team's optimizer. Across six evolutionary rounds per problem, this designated model reviews past transcripts, diagnoses why the team failed, and rewrites the strategy's roles, phases, and synthesis rules. When constructing the bank, SAT uses two safeguard mechanisms to prevent the system from creating rigid strategies that only work on a single training question. First, a separate instance of the reflecting model audits every proposed strategy to filter out candidates that encode specific answers, problem facts, or solution recipes. Second, any strategy that solves its training problem is held fixed and tested on five other training problems, called "validation probes." Strategies that generalize across these probes are scored, and the system freezes a final bank of up to 10 complementary strategies. At test-time deployment, the frozen bank transfers unchanged to unseen problems. For each new problem, the team runs all 10 strategies to produce 10 candidate "certificates": short, self-contained reasoning traces that can be checked step by step. A single judge model then reviews all 10 certificates and selects the best final answer. How SAT is trained and deployed (source: arXiv) For example, when experimenting SAT with GPQA science problems, during offline reflection, Gemini-2.5-Flash noticed that correct individual answers were repeatedly lost when the group rushed toward consensus. Observing that one of the agents was effective at challenging flawed assumptions, it created specialized audit strategies that required agents to resurface overlooked claims and audit specific peer steps before composing their answer. After passing the leakage screen and solving all five validation probes, these strategies were locked into the final bank. When deployed at test time on an unseen organic chemistry question, all three models initially guessed wrong answers on their own. Under the learned peer-audit strategy, Gemini challenged one of Llama's claims, realized its own mistake, and prompted Llama to revise its reasoning. Through this collaborative computation, the team reached the correct answer that none of its members had achieved independently. SAT in action and the "swarm tax" To evaluate SAT, the researchers trained two independent rosters of three models each and tested them on out-of-distribution benchmarks without modifying their strategy banks. The math-and-physics team (o3-mini, Claude Sonnet 4, and DeepSeek-V3) learned its bank on 15 AIME 2024 problems and was evaluated on held-out math and science questions. The knowledge-and-logic team (Gemini-2.5-Flash, Llama-4-Maverick, and GPT-4.1) learned its bank on 25 GPQA Diamond problems and transferred it to 100 unseen problems from industry benchmarks, including GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and BIG-Bench Extra Hard (BBEH). The researchers tested SAT against both single- and multi-agent baselines. Single-agent baselines included the strongest individual agent, 10-sample self-consistency, five-pass self-reflection, and a compute-matched "linearization" control that matched SAT but with a single strong model that serially executes every role and phase in the learned strategies by itself at roughly the same token budget. Multi-agent baselines included majority voting, three-round debate, Mixture of Agents, a homogeneous team (three copies of the strongest model running SAT's learned strategies), and a hypothetical "routing oracle" that always picks the right answer whenever one of the agents solves the problem alone. SAT results (source: arXiv) These controls directly address a growing concern for enterprise AI teams. In a recent article, we covered the " AI swarm tax ," based on research showing that when compute budgets are held equal, single agents often match or beat complex multi-agent systems because passing messages between agents consumes extra tokens and degrades context. The SAT study both validates that warning and shows how to overcome it. Where SAT aligns with the swarm tax study is in its homogeneous team control: when three identical copies of o3-mini executed the learned SAT strategies across the math and physics suite, average accuracy dropped to 56.0%, losing to a single o3-mini running compute-matched linearization (58.7%). Simply cloning a single model into a multi-agent workflow still wastes compute. Where SAT diverges is in combining model diversity with learned error repair. Across the math and physics benchmarks, the heterogeneous SAT roster averaged 66.7% accuracy, beating compute-matched linearization (58.7%), Mixture of Agents (57.3%), self-consistency (55.4%), and debate (52.7%). On AIME 2026, SAT reached 71.2% accuracy, beating the strongest individual member by 29 percentage points and exceeding the perfect routing oracle by 13.4 percentage points. One of the system’s learned strategies, dubbed “divergence_reconciliation” illustrates why model diversity matters. During training, the team observed that DeepSeek-V3 often found creative alternative derivations that caught edge cases other models missed, but also made frequent calculation errors. The learned strategy kept DeepSeek-V3 for initial diversity, but assigned o3-mini and Claude Sonnet 4 to independently verify DeepSeek's disputed steps. However, the knowledge-and-logic benchmarks revealed an important limitation for practitioners. While SAT achieved the highest average accuracy across GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and BBEH at 72.8%, it barely edged out single-agent linearization (72.1%) and fell short of the routing oracle (79.6%). The reason was that SAT generated at least one correct certificate on 87.9% of the knowledge-and-logic problems, beating the routing oracle on every benchmark. But the bottleneck became selecting the right answer from the pool, because the system struggled to reliably distinguish correct reasoning from plausible errors. When tasks involve verifiable, step-by-step logic like mathematics, physics, or code, valid corrections survive peer audits and get selected. On softer knowledge tasks where wrong explanations still sound convincing, the final judge struggles to separate correct insights from confident hallucinations. Implementing SAT in the enterprise While the researchers have not released an official code repository, the paper's appendices provide a detailed blueprint for engineering teams looking to build self-organizing workflows. The researchers have provided the prompts, role definitions, and phase rules for all 20 learned strategies across the domains they experimented. Developers can take the proven and implement them inside their orchestration frameworks. The researchers also provide the two-stage system prompts used by the judge model. For enterprise teams designing their own multi-agent systems, the study offers two practical guidelines: Blind model identities during reflection: When using a model to review transcripts and assign roles, mask the underlying model names. This ensures the system assigns roles based on observed behavioral strengths instead of pretrained biases about specific model brands.

Match inference compute to task verifiability: Running a full bank of 10 multi-round strategies per query requires substantial test-time compute. Teams should reserve the full 10-strategy ensemble for high-stakes, highly demonstrable problems such as automated vulnerability analysis or formal system design, while adapting one or two targeted audit strategies for everyday workflows. "More broadly, our results position organization itself as an agent capability: without human-specified problem decompositions, a fixed set of models can learn to reason together and construct solutions unavailable to any member independently," the researchers write.

data.title: Open Weight AI Is Moving the Competitive Advantage From Models to Inference
data.ai_summary: Meta released Muse Glimmer, a compact open-weight model for single-GPU devices, and plans to open Muse Spark 1.2 weights. IBM and Together AI signed a $240 million agreement to build an inference cluster on IBM Cloud. The shift moves competitive advantage from model training to inference deployment and operation.
data.full_text:
On 10 August, Meta released Muse Glimmer, a compact open-weight model designed to handle reasoning and agentic tasks on a Mac or PC equipped with a single graphics card. Glimmer was distilled from Meta's more capable Muse Spark model, and Meta says it also plans to release the weights of Muse Spark 1.2.
The important part is not simply that Meta released another model. It is that the model can leave Meta's infrastructure.
That distinction points to a broader shift in AI. For the past several years, the industry has treated the foundation model as its centre of gravity. Whoever trained the most capable system appeared to control the stack. Enterprises rented intelligence through APIs, start-ups built products around those APIs, and governments worried about which countries possessed frontier models.
Open-weight AI is weakening that assumption.
Meta is not alone in recognising the opportunity. IBM and Together AI recently signed a $240 million multi-year agreement to build a large inference cluster on IBM Cloud using Nvidia HGX B300 systems. The initial deployment is expected to use roughly 2,000 Blackwell chips and support open-model inference workloads.
These developments illustrate the same shift from opposite ends of the stack. Meta is making model capability more portable. IBM and Together AI are building the infrastructure required to operate portable models at scale.
The strategic question is therefore changing. It is no longer only: who can train the best model? Increasingly, it is: who can deploy, adapt, route and operate models most effectively?
The model is becoming one layer of the stack
Foundation models will not disappear. Training the most capable systems still requires extraordinary capital, compute, data and engineering talent. Stanford's 2026 AI Index found that industry produced more than 90% of notable frontier models in 2025.
What is changing is what happens after a model has been trained.
A model contains capability. Inference turns that capability into a reliable service. That requires far more than loading weights onto a GPU. The operational layer includes serving engines, quantisation, batching, request scheduling, caching and model routing. It also includes access controls, fallback policies, monitoring and the evaluation systems needed to decide whether a response was useful enough to justify its cost.
Every one of those choices affects the service delivered to a user. Quantisation may reduce memory requirements but alter output quality. Batching can improve throughput while increasing latency. Caching can lower cost but creates questions about freshness and data separation. Routing can send routine work to an efficient model and reserve a more capable model for difficult cases, but only if the system can recognise which case it is handling.
Open weights make this operational layer more strategically important because they separate a model from its original provider.
OpenAI, for example, makes its gpt-oss models available under the Apache 2.0 licence. Organisations can run them on infrastructure they control, use an independent hosting provider, and adapt or fine-tune them. The weights carry no API fee, although operators still pay for compute, storage, engineering, security and hosting.
Open weights do not make intelligence free. They make it portable.
Portability changes the economics
An API bundles a model with infrastructure, security controls, updates, pricing and a commercial relationship. That simplicity has real value, but it also gives the provider control over variables such as prices, model retirement, usage policies and where workloads run.
With downloadable weights, organisations gain another option. They can operate a model themselves, use an independent inference provider, fine-tune it for a specialised task, or move it between infrastructure providers.
That creates competition around a different question: how cheaply and reliably can a model be turned into useful work?
The IBM–Together AI agreement suggests that businesses already see inference as a significant infrastructure market. Together AI was valued at $8.3 billion in July, and the IBM cluster is explicitly intended to provide production-scale open-model inference.
This is also why model routing matters. A company processing insurance claims does not need the strongest reasoning model for every document. A small model might extract standard fields. A specialised model might detect anomalies. Only an uncertain or unusually complex case may justify an expensive frontier system.
For enterprises, portability must be designed into the application. Business logic should not be tightly coupled to one provider's endpoint or response format. Teams need model-independent interfaces, task-level evaluation suites, standardised telemetry and explicit data boundaries.
They should also measure what matters operationally: cost per successful task, p95 latency, error rate, fallback frequency and the proportion of cases requiring human review. A cheaper model is not cheaper if its failures create more manual work. A faster model is not faster if unreliable output delays the wider process.
The aim is not to swap models constantly. It is to preserve the option when economics, performance, policy or risk changes.
Once several models can solve the same routine task, benchmark leadership becomes only one consideration alongside cost, latency, privacy, reliability and switching friction. Models do not become irrelevant, but they become more substitutable for particular workloads.
Sovereign AI is also an infrastructure question
Governments are reaching a similar conclusion.
Sovereign AI is often presented as a race to build national foundation models. Yet owning a model achieves little if a country lacks the compute, energy, skills and deployment infrastructure required to run it.
The UK's Compute Roadmap commits more than £1 billion to expand the AI Research Resource twentyfold by 2030 and supports a Sovereign AI Unit with up to £500 million. The roadmap treats domestic compute capacity as strategic infrastructure rather than an incidental input.
A government does not need to invent every model it uses. It does need enough control over compute, data, deployment and procurement to retain meaningful choices.
Open weights can help. They allow a country or regulated organisation to run a foreign-developed model under domestic jurisdiction rather than sending sensitive data permanently through a foreign API. They may also make it easier to inspect, adapt and replace a model when requirements change.
But open weights do not eliminate dependence. Chips, energy, cloud infrastructure, networking and engineering talent remain concentrated resources. The Center for a New American Security's Sovereign AI Index tracks national projects across infrastructure, models and data, with infrastructure representing the largest category.
Sovereignty is therefore less about owning every component than maintaining credible alternatives across the stack.
The safety objection is real
There is a powerful argument against pushing this logic too far.
Once capable weights circulate, the original developer loses many of the controls available through an API. Users can alter safeguards, fine-tune behaviour or operate models without central monitoring. OpenAI itself notes that determined attackers can fine-tune open-weight models to bypass refusals in ways that a developer can no longer revoke centrally.
Government testing shows why this matters. The UK AI Security Institute found that GLM-5.2, released in June 2026, was the most cyber-capable open-weight model it had tested at the time. It performed similarly to leading closed models released roughly four to seven months earlier. That gap had narrowed from the six-to-ten-month lag the institute measured through much of 2025.
This is not a minor concern. Wider access to capable weights can widen access to harmful capabilities as well.
However, it does not follow that the only safe approach is to keep intelligence permanently tied to a handful of APIs. Risk also depends on what tools a model can access, how much compute it receives, whether it can act autonomously, what data it can reach and where it is deployed.
Safety policy therefore has to follow the architecture. Organisations need capability evaluations, secure infrastructure, model provenance, deployment controls, least-privilege tool access, monitoring and clear accountability for high-risk uses. Those controls matter whether the underlying model is open-weight or closed.
Build for a world of more interchangeable intelligence
Executives should stop designing AI systems around the assumption that one model provider will remain central forever.
Applications should allow models to be replaced without rebuilding the surrounding workflow. Teams should measure business outcomes rather than relying on benchmark reputation. Efficient models can handle routine work, while expensive frontier systems are reserved for problems that genuinely require them. Proprietary data, customer workflows and evaluation systems should remain separate from any single model vendor.
Policymakers should make the same adjustment. Investment is needed not only in models, but also in compute capacity, interoperability, evaluation infrastructure, open standards and the ability to move workloads between providers. Sovereignty should mean retaining meaningful options, not attempting to build every component domestically.
Engineers, meanwhile, should treat the model as a component rather than the whole architecture.
The foundation model remains important, but it is no longer the entire strategy. Competitive advantage is moving towards the systems that select, adapt, evaluate and operate models effectively.
The next contest in AI will not only be about who creates intelligence. It will be about who can put that intelligence to work reliably, safely and economically.

data.full_text:
Together AI has released Together Link, a free, MIT-licensed CLI now in beta. It connects the coding agents developers already use to open models hosted on Together AI. Supported tools include Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, ChatGPT Desktop, OpenCode, and Pi. The idea is simple: keep the harness, swap the model, and shrink the bill.

Is it deployable today? Yes. It installs with one command on macOS or Linux and needs only a Together API key. It is in beta, so commands, routing, and the model list may change.

The Problem It Targets

Coding agents often send every task to the same premium model, from a one-line fix to a full rewrite. In its launch post, Together team states that engineering orgs spend tens of thousands to millions of dollars monthly on closed models. Its argument is that open models have closed much of the gap. Kimi K3 and GLM 5.3 target hard coding work. GLM 5.3 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash cover everyday tasks.

How Together Link Works

Installation is a single command:

Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser curl - fsSL https :

The installer adds Bun if needed and places commands in ~/.local/bin . Run togetherlink to open a launcher, or start a tool directly with togetherlink claude , togetherlink codex , togetherlink opencode , or togetherlink pi . Shortcuts such as tclaude also work.

According to the official docs, no local proxy or daemon runs. Each tool talks directly to Together’s hosted gateway. Terminal agents receive a temporary per-launch configuration that is removed when the session ends. Claude Desktop and ChatGPT Desktop use separate, reversible profiles. Commands like togetherlink chatgpt off switch back.

The Auto Router

Sessions default to a virtual auto model. Per the launch post, the router reads each session’s first task. Quick fixes go to fast, low-cost models, while hard problems get frontier capability. With an Anthropic API key, it routes between Opus 5.5 and GLM 5.3. Without one, it routes between GLM 5.3 and GLM 5.3 Flash. Routing happens once per session, so prompt caching keeps working.

The Opus path applies only to Claude Code and Claude Desktop, billed to your Anthropic account. Codex, OpenCode, Pi, and ChatGPT Desktop always stay on Together models. To pin one model, place the flag before the tool name: togetherlink --main zai-org/GLM-5.3 claude .

Inside Claude Code, the /model menu maps tiers to open models. Opus runs Kimi K3, Fable runs GLM 5.3, Sonnet runs GLM 5.3 Flash, and Haiku runs DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.

Models, Pricing, and Receipts

The docs list Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, each with 1M context. The product page lists Kimi K3 at $3.00 in and $15.00 out, and GLM 5.3 at $1.40 in and $4.40 out. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and MiniMax M3 are listed at $0.30 in and $1.20 out. Current rates live on Together’s pricing page.

Billing runs on your existing Together key, through pay-as-you-go or credit packs. Each session prints token and dollar totals on exit. In Claude Code, the status line shows estimated spend beside the equivalent Opus cost. Running togetherlink usage --last 7d shows gateway-tracked spend across sessions.

Together team also notes it serves the largest OpenRouter token share for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (40.8%), GLM 5.3 Flash (28.2%), and Kimi K3 (23.1%), as of 9/30/2026.

data.full_text: Clockwork.io has raised $31 million in new funding to expand its fault-tolerance software for artificial intelligence infrastructure, bringing total funding to $73 million. The round was co-led by Premji Invest, Wing Venture Capital and Seligman Ventures, with participation from existing investors NEA and e& Capital. Clockwork.io plans to use the financing to accelerate deployment of its fault-tolerance technology across AI training, inference and reinforcement learning, expand enterprise adoption and scale distribution through cloud partners. The company also announced production deployments at LinkedIn and Together AI and an expanded relationship with WhiteFiber. Clockwork.io develops software designed to keep large distributed AI workloads running when GPUs, network links or servers fail. Its LinkPass product reroutes network traffic around failed links, while TorchPass moves workloads from failing GPUs to healthy hardware rather than requiring a job to restart from an earlier checkpoint. The company introduced two additional TorchPass capabilities alongside the financing. Multi-node platform snapshots capture the state of a distributed AI job across all of its nodes without requiring changes to the training code, allowing the workload to be restored following a major failure. Clockwork.io also introduced asynchronous application checkpoints that operate in the background while jobs continue running. The feature is designed in part to accelerate reinforcement learning by delivering updated model weights to inference replicas more quickly. LinkedIn has deployed LinkPass across its AI infrastructure fleet and says the technology prevents tens of thousands of GPU-hours of downtime each month. Together AI plans to offer TorchPass as a service on its GPU Clusters, while WhiteFiber is expanding Clockwork.io across its global GPU-as-a-service infrastructure. Clockwork.io said its approach addresses a growing infrastructure challenge as AI jobs expand across thousands of GPUs and individual hardware or networking problems can disrupt an entire workload. KEY QUOTES: “Failures are inevitable at AI scale. Losing hours of useful work to them should not be. Fault tolerance is a goodput multiplier: it keeps GPUs doing useful work instead of waiting for recovery or repeating work already done. We built our software alongside enterprises and cloud providers operating some of the largest GPU fleets, so it handles the failures they actually see. That protection belongs in the infrastructure enterprises and cloud providers rely on every day.” Suresh Vasudevan, CEO of Clockwork.io “At AI infrastructure scale, a single network issue should never sideline healthy GPUs or interrupt running workloads. Before Clockwork.io, one InfiniBand NIC flap could remove an eight-GPU server from service, while a switch port flap could drain a second server, doubling the impact to 16 GPUs. Clockwork.io helped transform that operating model. Its network fault-tolerance technology automatically reroutes traffic onto healthy paths, allowing jobs to continue uninterrupted while link, optic, cable, or NIC faults are repaired. In aggregate, Clockwork.io prevents tens of thousands of GPU-hours of downtime per month across our fleet. By turning what were once disruptive operational incidents into manageable maintenance events, Clockwork.io has helped improve infrastructure utilization and operational efficiency.” Raghu Hiremagalur, SVP and CTO Infrastructure at LinkedIn “Our customers grade us on goodput, the share of their GPU-hours that actually move the model forward. Node repair already detects faults and provisions replacement capacity automatically. Clockwork.io’s TorchPass and LinkPass build on that foundation and are designed to keep jobs moving through GPU faults and link failures, preserving progress. We are bringing them to market as the next layer of resilience in the platform.” Pavneet Ahluwalia, Product Lead at Together AI “Pressure-testing a cluster’s reliability before it reaches production is critical, because a customer who inherits a hidden fabric fault pays for it later in failed jobs and lost GPU-hours. Marginal optics, misconfigured NICs, and links that pass a basic test but degrade under load can slip through. Clockwork.io’s automated fleet audit validates every link and node at once, localizes faults in minutes, and lets us correct them before acceptance. We bring clusters up faster, and a customer’s first training run lands on a fabric validated end-to-end, not just powered on. With market demand growing as rapidly as it is, getting validated capacity to customers quickly is critical to our business, and it is why we are expanding Clockwork.io across our clusters.” Tom Sanfilippo, Chief Technology Officer of WhiteFiber “Cluster fault tolerance used to be a training problem. It is now an inference problem too. In our ClusterMAX, TorchPass cuts training goodput loss from 14% to under 3% for a gold-rated neocloud. Reinforcement Learning (RL) ties the two together: inference replicas generate rollouts, the trainer learns from them, and the updated weights go back to the replicas. Clockwork.io keeps replicas serving through link flaps and network failures. Its extremely fast checkpoints accelerate weight transfer back into the rollout fleet, so neither direction stalls the run. One fault-tolerance layer under training, inference, and RL is where this has to be solved.” Dylan Patel, Founder, CEO and Chief Analyst at SemiAnalysis “The one thing that scales perfectly is unreliability: put enough GPUs in one machine and something is always failing. The old playbook: stop the job, reload a checkpoint, makes no sense at today’s scale. Clockwork treats failure as the normal state: TorchPass migrates training off a failing GPU live, and now snapshots an entire running job with no code changes. It’s already saving tens of thousands of GPU-hours a month. We first backed Clockwork.io in 2021 and are thrilled to keep supporting them as they define the performance layer of the AI cluster.” Greg Papadopoulos, Venture Partner at NEA Thank you for visiting Pulse 2.0. PALO ALTO, California, 5 de octubre de 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Clockwork.io, cuyo software de tolerancia a fallos mantiene en funcionamiento las cargas de trabajo de entrenamiento de IA, aprendizaje por refuerzo e inferencia ante fallos de infraestructura, anunció hoy una nueva financiación de 31 millones de dólares, despliegues en producción en LinkedIn y Together AI, y una mayor adopción por parte de WhiteFiber. Continue Reading

New TorchPass innovations preserve AI workload progress without code changes and speed reinforcement learning. La empresa también presentó dos nuevas funcionalidades para su solución TorchPass, cada una de las cuales captura el estado de una tarea de IA distribuida en ejecución. Las instantáneas de plataforma multimodo, una primicia en el sector para la formación, guardan la tarea completa en todos los nodos sin necesidad de modificar el código de entrenamiento y la preservan para su posterior recuperación. Por su parte, los puntos de control de aplicación rápidos y asíncronos, que se realizan en segundo plano mientras la tarea está en curso, aceleran el aprendizaje por refuerzo. Estos suministran pesos del modelo actualizados a las réplicas de inferencia encargadas de generar los rollouts, los ejemplos a partir de los cuales aprende el modelo, lo que permite que dichas réplicas pasen menos tiempo esperando o trabajando con un modelo desactualizado. La tolerancia a fallos se ha convertido en un requisito para la IA a gran escala Las grandes cargas de trabajo de IA distribuida pueden abarcar miles de GPU que deben mantenerse sincronizadas: el fallo de una sola GPU, la interrupción de un enlace o el bloqueo de un servidor pueden paralizar la tarea por completo. Meta informó de interrupciones inesperadas con una frecuencia media aproximada de una cada tres horas durante un periodo de 54 días de entrenamiento de Llama 3 utilizando 16.384 GPU. La respuesta habitual consiste en recargar un punto de control, es decir, una copia guardada del progreso de la tarea. El proceso de recuperación puede durar hasta 90 minutos, deja inactivas las GPU que funcionan correctamente y obliga a repetir el trabajo realizado desde dicho punto de control. Los clientes pagan por GPU ociosas y por cálculos redundantes, y los modelos tardan más en completarse. A medida que las tareas aumentan de tamaño, cada reinicio pone en riesgo una mayor cantidad de tiempo de uso de las GPU. A esta escala, garantizar la continuidad del trabajo útil a pesar de los fallos es un requisito de infraestructura. Clockwork.io satisface esta necesidad mediante un conjunto de herramientas de tolerancia a fallos que los equipos de plataforma despliegan como una capa intermedia entre el hardware y la carga de trabajo. LinkPass redirige el tráfico para evitar el enlace averiado, de modo que la tarea no llega a detectar el fallo. TorchPass transfiere la carga de trabajo de una GPU defectuosa a una operativa, permitiendo que el entrenamiento continúe sin necesidad de retroceder a un estado anterior. Ambas soluciones están ya en fase de producción. La nueva funcionalidad de snapshots de plataforma de TorchPass, anunciada hoy, captura el estado de una tarea distribuida en ejecución; esto permite restaurar la tarea completa cuando el fallo es demasiado grave para solucionarlo mediante una simple migración. "Los fallos son inevitables a la escala de la IA; perder horas de trabajo útil debido a ellos no debería ocurrir", afirmó Suresh Vasudevan, consejero delegado de Clockwork.io. "La tolerancia a fallos actúa como un multiplicador del rendimiento útil: permite que las GPU sigan realizando trabajo productivo en lugar de esperar a procesos de recuperación o repetir tareas ya completadas. Desarrollamos nuestro software en colaboración con empresas y proveedores de nube que operan algunas de las mayores flotas de GPU, por lo que es capaz de gestionar los fallos que realmente experimentan. Esa protección debe formar parte de la infraestructura de la que dependen a diario dichas empresas y proveedores". La adopción se extiende a empresas, hiperescaladores y neoclouds Las empresas que gestionan sus propias flotas de GPU, así como los hiperescaladores y los proveedores de "neocloud", están adoptando Clockwork.io por la misma razón: logran que una mayor parte de sus horas de GPU se destine a trabajo útil. LinkedIn ha implementado la tolerancia a fallos de red LinkPass en toda su flota de infraestructura de IA, evitando así la pérdida de decenas de miles de horas de GPU por inactividad cada mes. "A escala de infraestructura de IA, un único problema de red nunca debería dejar fuera de servicio a GPUs que funcionan correctamente ni interrumpir las cargas de trabajo en ejecución. Antes de Clockwork.io, una oscilación en InfiniBand NIC podía retirar del servicio un servidor con ocho GPU, mientras que una oscilación en el puerto de un conmutador podía dejar inoperativo un segundo servidor, duplicando el impacto a 16 GPU", afirmó Raghu Hiremagalur, vicepresidente sénior y director de tecnología de Infraestructura en LinkedIn. "Clockwork.io ayudó a transformar ese modelo operativo. Su tecnología de tolerancia a fallos de red redirige automáticamente el tráfico hacia rutas operativas, permitiendo que las tareas continúen sin interrupciones mientras se reparan los fallos en enlaces, componentes ópticos, cables o tarjetas de red. En conjunto, Clockwork.io evita decenas de miles de horas de inactividad de GPU al mes en toda nuestra flota. Al convertir lo que antes eran incidentes operativos disruptivos en eventos de mantenimiento manejables, Clockwork.io ha contribuido a mejorar la utilización de la infraestructura y la eficiencia operativa". Together AI lanza TorchPass al mercado como un servicio en sus clústeres de GPU. Durante la conferencia PyTorch, ambas empresas realizarán una demostración en vivo de una tarea de entrenamiento multinodo que continúa ejecutándose —sin necesidad de reinicio— a pesar de la introducción deliberada de fallos en la red y en las GPU. "Nuestros clientes nos evalúan en función del goodput, es decir, la proporción de sus horas de GPU que realmente hacen avanzar el modelo", afirmó Pavneet Ahluwalia, responsable de producto de Together AI. "La función de reparación de nodos ya detecta fallos y aprovisiona capacidad de sustitución de forma automática. Las soluciones TorchPass y LinkPass de Clockwork.io se basan en esa infraestructura y están diseñadas para mantener la ejecución de las tareas a pesar de los fallos de GPU y de enlace, preservando así el progreso realizado. Las estamos lanzando al mercado como la siguiente capa de resiliencia de la plataforma". WhiteFiber (NASDAQ: WYFI), cliente actual de la compañía, está ampliando el uso del software de Clockwork.io en su creciente infraestructura global de GPU como servicio. "Someter a pruebas de estrés la fiabilidad de un clúster antes de que pase a producción es fundamental, ya que el cliente que recibe un sistema con un fallo oculto en la red de interconexión acaba pagando las consecuencias en forma de trabajos fallidos y horas de GPU perdidas", afirmó Tom Sanfilippo, director de tecnología de WhiteFiber. "Componentes ópticos de calidad marginal, tarjetas de red (NIC) mal configuradas y enlaces que superan una prueba básica pero se degradan bajo carga pueden pasar desapercibidos. La auditoría automatizada de flotas de Clockwork.io valida simultáneamente cada enlace y nodo, localiza fallos en cuestión de minutos y nos permite corregirlos antes de la entrega. Ponemos los clústeres en marcha con mayor rapidez, de modo que la primera ejecución de entrenamiento del cliente se realiza sobre una red validada de extremo a extremo, y no simplemente sobre un sistema encendido. Dada la vertiginosa demanda del mercado, ofrecer a los clientes capacidad validada con rapidez es crucial para nuestro negocio; por eso estamos implementando Clockwork.io en todos nuestros clústeres". Las nuevas funcionalidades de TorchPass ponen la protección de las cargas de trabajo en manos de los equipos de plataforma Clockwork.io ha ampliado las capacidades de TorchPass más allá de la migración de GPU, incorporando dos funciones de las que los equipos de plataforma carecían hasta ahora: la posibilidad de generar ellos mismos una instantánea de todo un trabajo distribuido y puntos de control de la aplicación lo suficientemente rápidos como para ejecutarse en segundo plano. En el caso del entrenamiento, las instantáneas de la plataforma guardan el estado de ejecución de un trabajo en curso en todos sus nodos, permitiendo así restaurarlo tras una interrupción. Los equipos de plataforma e ingenieros de infraestructura de IA implementan esta solución para cargas de trabajo compatibles sin necesidad de que los propietarios de las aplicaciones modifiquen su código o añadan lógica de puntos de control. Los equipos empresariales pueden proteger los trabajos de entrenamiento en toda su flota mediante un único mecanismo, y los proveedores de nube pueden proteger los trabajos de los clientes cuyo código no controlan. Cuando los equipos implementan puntos de control a nivel de aplicación, la rapidez de los puntos de control de TorchPass permite realizarlos con mayor frecuencia; de este modo, se pierde menos progreso y se repite menos trabajo de cómputo tras un fallo. En cuanto a la inferencia, los modelos de gran tamaño se ejecutan en dos o más servidores, por lo que un fallo en un enlace puede inutilizar una réplica completa e interrumpir una sesión de usuario o una tarea de agente en plena ejecución. LinkPass permite que dichas réplicas multiservidor sigan operativas a pesar de los fallos en los enlaces. El aprendizaje por refuerzo depende tanto del entrenamiento como de la inferencia. Varias copias del modelo generan secuencias de ejecución, el sistema de entrenamiento aprende de ellas y los pesos actualizados deben llegar a las copias antes de que estas puedan generar resultados con la versión más reciente. Los puntos de control de aplicación de TorchPass transfieren los pesos actualizados a las réplicas de ejecución con mayor rapidez, mientras que LinkPass mantiene dichas réplicas en funcionamiento a pesar de los fallos en los enlaces. "La tolerancia a fallos en clústeres solía ser un problema exclusivo del entrenamiento; ahora es también un problema de inferencia", afirmó Dylan Patel, fundador, consejero delegado y analista principal de SemiAnalysis, empresa cuyas clasificaciones ClusterMAX evalúan a los proveedores de servicios en la nube basados en GPU. "En nuestras pruebas ClusterMAX, TorchPass reduce la pérdida de rendimiento efectivo durante el entrenamiento del 14 % a menos del 3 % en un proveedor neocloud con calificación "oro". El aprendizaje por refuerzo (RL) vincula ambos procesos: las réplicas de inferencia generan simulaciones, el sistema de entrenamiento aprende de ellas y los pesos actualizados regresan a las réplicas. Clockwork.io permite que las réplicas sigan operando a pesar de las fluctuaciones de enlace y los fallos de red. Sus puntos de control ultrarrápidos aceleran la transferencia de pesos de vuelta a la flota de inferencia, evitando así que el proceso se detenga en cualquiera de las dos direcciones. La solución debe implementarse mediante una capa de tolerancia a fallos común para el entrenamiento, la inferencia y el aprendizaje por refuerzo". Los equipos de plataformas empresariales y los proveedores de servicios en la nube pueden ponerse en contacto con Clockwork.io para evaluar el software en sus cargas de trabajo o explorar oportunidades de colaboración. La ronda de financiación y su destino La ronda fue coliderada por Premji Invest, Wing Venture Capital y Seligman Ventures, con la participación de los inversores actuales NEA y e& Capital. Con esto, la financiación total de Clockwork.io alcanza los 73 millones de dólares. La empresa utilizará el capital para acelerar el despliegue de su conjunto de herramientas de tolerancia a fallos —aplicable a las fases de entrenamiento, inferencia y aprendizaje por refuerzo—, ampliar su adopción empresarial y escalar la entrega a través de socios en la nube. "Lo único que escala a la perfección es la falta de fiabilidad: basta con instalar suficientes GPU en una máquina para que siempre haya algo fallando", afirmó Greg Papadopoulos, socio de capital riesgo de NEA. "El método tradicional —detener la tarea y recargar un punto de control— carece de sentido a la escala actual. Clockwork considera el fallo como el estado habitual: TorchPass migra en tiempo real el entrenamiento desde una GPU que presenta errores y ahora permite capturar el estado de toda una tarea en ejecución sin necesidad de modificar el código. Ya está ahorrando decenas de miles de horas de GPU al mes. Apostamos por Clockwork.io en 2021 y estamos encantados de seguir apoyándolos mientras definen la capa de rendimiento de los clústeres de IA". Acerca de Clockwork.io Clockwork.io es pionera en Software-Driven AI Fabrics™, una capa programable situada entre el hardware y la carga de trabajo que permite que los clústeres de GPU sean observables, tolerantes a fallos y aprovechen al máximo su capacidad, independientemente del acelerador, la red o la nube utilizados. Las cargas de trabajo de IA requieren que todo el clúster funcione como una única máquina; sin embargo, los fallos y los cuellos de botella dejan las GPU inactivas. La plataforma FleetLens de Clockwork.io recupera esa capacidad perdida: gracias a una telemetría con precisión de nanosegundos, identifica exactamente qué GPU, nodo o enlace está ralentizando o bloqueando una tarea y valida los clústeres antes de su puesta en marcha. Además, mediante LinkPass y TorchPass, garantiza la continuidad de las cargas de trabajo —desde el entrenamiento hasta la inferencia— incluso ante fallos o degradaciones de la infraestructura. Según pruebas comparativas independientes realizadas por SemiAnalysis, TorchPass supera a los principales marcos de trabajo de código abierto y a los métodos tradicionales de punto de control y reinicio en cuanto a la velocidad de recuperación ante fallos. Empresas como LinkedIn, Together AI, WhiteFiber, Wells Fargo, Nebius, NScale y DCAI confían en Clockwork.io para impulsar su infraestructura de IA. Más información en www.clockwork.io.

For AI startups, choosing a model isn’t necessarily a one-time architecture decision anymore.

Open models are improving. Frontier APIs keep advancing. Models can be customized for specific workloads, and some companies are building products that use multiple models rather than committing to one. That gives founders more ways to build — and more decisions about where to spend, what to own, and how much flexibility to preserve as the technology changes.

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, four conversations approach those decisions from different points in the AI stack, from multi-model applications and customized models to infrastructure and the chips underneath them.

When one AI model isn’t enough

Choosing between open and proprietary models assumes a company needs to choose one in the first place. Increasingly, AI products can call on different models for different jobs.

The session “The Real Tokenmaxxing: How the Best AI Companies Navigate a Multi-Model World” will bring together Mo Jomaa, partner at CapitalG; Vipul Ved Prakash, co-founder and CEO of Together AI; and Zuzanna Stamirowska, CEO and co-founder of Pathway, on the Builder’s Stage.

They’ll explore why companies are using multiple models; how they balance cost, performance, and flexibility; and when open models can outperform proprietary alternatives.

How much of your AI stack should you own?

Model choice also raises a bigger question: What does your company need to own?

Manos Koukoumidis, CEO and co-founder of Oumi, will take the Real World AI Stage for “Which AI Should Your Company Actually Deploy: Rent, Customize, or Build.” He’ll tackle whether startups should build their own models, when customization can become a competitive advantage, and how to choose between open and proprietary AI.

Through audience polls, startup scenarios, and a practical framework, Koukoumidis will help attendees evaluate frontier APIs, customized open weights, and owning AI outright. Attendees will come away with three decision principles they can bring to their next architecture conversation.

The choice founders make can shape both the product and the business behind it. Building more of the AI stack can offer greater control and differentiation, but it can also require more time, talent, and resources than relying on existing models.

Where open and proprietary AI fit

When architecture reaches the hardware

Model architecture is only part of the equation. AI performance ultimately depends on the hardware underneath it, and advances in AI are beginning to change how that hardware gets designed.

Anna Goldie, founder and CEO of Ricursive Intelligence, and Azalia Mirhoseini, founder and CTO, will take that idea to the Disrupt Stage in “When AI Starts Designing Its Own Hardware.” They’ll explore how AI is optimizing chips and hardware, why model architecture and hardware are becoming more closely connected, and what an increasingly open AI ecosystem could mean for the infrastructure underneath it.

The Challenge of GPU Downtime

Clockwork.io has raised $31 million in new funding as the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure exposes an expensive weakness: thousands of GPUs can sit idle when a single component fails.
The round was co-led by Premji Invest, Wing Ventures and Seligman Ventures, with participation from existing investors NEA and e& Capital. The company is targeting a problem that becomes more costly as AI models and clusters grow. Meta previously reported unexpected interruptions roughly every three hours during a 54-day Llama 3 training run involving 16,384 GPUs.
Meet the team behind Clockwork
Clockwork.io was founded in 2018 from Stanford research by Balaji Prabhakar, Yilong Geng and Deepak Merugu, with Mendel Rosenblum, the VMware co-founder, serving as chief scientist. Prabhakar is a Stanford professor whose research focuses on computer networks and data-centre systems, while Geng’s Stanford research produced the Huygens clock-synchronisation technology that became foundational to Clockwork’s platform. Merugu previously co-founded Urban Engines, which was acquired by Google.
The company is now led by Suresh Vasudevan, who joined as CEO after leading Sysdig and Nimble Storage. At Nimble, he took the company through an IPO and its eventual acquisition by HPE. He also held senior leadership roles at NetApp.
From GPU failures to live recovery
Clockwork’s argument is that conventional checkpoint-and-restart systems are increasingly inefficient for large distributed AI workloads.
A failed GPU, network link, NIC or server can force an entire training job to restart from its last checkpoint, potentially losing hours of completed work and leaving healthy GPUs idle.
Clockwork’s software sits between infrastructure and workloads to keep jobs running through those failures.
LinkPass reroutes network traffic around failed links, while TorchPass moves workloads from failing GPUs to healthy ones without requiring a complete restart. TorchSnap adds another layer by capturing the state of distributed AI jobs across multiple nodes.

Clockwork is attacking a different layer of the same infrastructure stack: ensuring that the enormous amount of compute being deployed actually gets used.
With AI clusters becoming larger, more expensive and harder to keep synchronised, Clockwork’s bet is that resilience will become as important as raw GPU performance.

It is now an inference problem too," said Dylan Patel, Founder, CEO, and Chief Analyst at SemiAnalysis, whose ClusterMAX ratings benchmark GPU cloud providers. "In our ClusterMAX, TorchPass cuts training goodput loss from 14% to under 3% for a gold-rated neocloud. Reinforcement Learning (RL) ties the two together: inference replicas generate rollouts, the trainer learns from them, and the updated weights go back to the replicas. Clockwork.io keeps replicas serving through link flaps and network failures. Its extremely fast checkpoints accelerate weight transfer back into the rollout fleet, so neither direction stalls the run. One fault-tolerance layer under training, inference, and RL is where this has to be solved." Enterprise platform teams and cloud providers can contact Clockwork.io to evaluate the software for their workloads or explore partnership opportunities. The round and what it funds The round was co-led by Premji Invest, Wing Venture Capital, and Seligman Ventures, with participation from existing investors NEA and e& Capital. It brings Clockwork.io's total funding to $73 million. The company will use the capital to accelerate the rollout of its fault-tolerance suite across training, inference and reinforcement learning, expand enterprise adoption, and scale delivery through cloud partners. "The one thing that scales perfectly is unreliability: put enough GPUs in one machine and something is always failing," said Greg Papadopoulos, Venture Partner, NEA. "The old playbook: stop the job, reload a checkpoint, makes no sense at today's scale. Clockwork treats failure as the normal state: TorchPass migrates training off a failing GPU live, and now snapshots an entire running job with no code changes. It's already saving tens of thousands of GPU-hours a month. We first backed Clockwork.io in 2021 and are thrilled to keep supporting them as they define the performance layer of the AI cluster." About Clockwork.io Clockwork.io pioneers Software-Driven AI Fabrics™, a programmable layer between hardware and workload that makes GPU clusters observable, fault-tolerant, and fully utilized across any accelerator, network, or cloud. AI workloads need the whole cluster to act as one machine, yet failures and bottlenecks idle GPUs. Clockwork.io's FleetLens platform recovers that lost capacity: nanosecond-accurate telemetry pinpoints the GPU, node, or link slowing or stalling a job, validates clusters before launch, and, with LinkPass and TorchPass, keeps workloads running through infrastructure failures and degradations, from training to inference. SemiAnalysis has independently benchmarked TorchPass as recovering from failures faster than checkpoint-restart and leading open-source frameworks. Multi-Node-Plattform-Snapshots – eine Branchenneuheit für das Training – speichern einen gesamten laufenden Job über alle Knoten hinweg ohne Änderungen am Trainingscode und bewahren ihn für die Wiederherstellung auf. Schnelle, asynchrone Anwendungs-Checkpoints, die im Hintergrund während der Ausführung des Jobs erstellt werden, beschleunigen das verstärkende Lernen. Sie liefern aktualisierte Modellgewichte an die Inferenz-Replikate, die „Rollouts" generieren – also die Beispiele, aus denen das Modell lernt –, sodass diese Replikate weniger Zeit damit verbringen, zu warten oder mit einem veralteten Modell zu arbeiten. Fehlertoleranz ist zu einer Voraussetzung für KI in großem Maßstab geworden Große verteilte KI-Workloads können sich über Tausende von GPUs erstrecken, die synchron bleiben müssen: Eine ausgefallene GPU, eine unterbrochene Verbindung oder ein eingefrorener Server kann den gesamten Job zum Stillstand bringen.
